# Appendix A — The Plackett–Luce objective in torch {#sec-appx-a}

Paper 3 implements the depth-$k$ Plackett–Luce likelihood as a custom
XGBoost objective with an analytic gradient and Hessian. This paper needs
the same likelihood as a differentiable loss over padded, variable-length
race batches. A second implementation of a likelihood is a place where a
series quietly stops comparing like with like, so it is verified against the
first rather than trusted.

## The loss

A batch is a set of whole races, padded to that batch's widest field. For
each race $r$ with $J_r$ runners, scores $z_{rj}$ and $S = \min(k, J_r - 1)$
scoring stages, the negative log-likelihood is

$$
\ell_r \;=\; -\sum_{s=1}^{S}\Big[ z_{r,(s)} \;-\; \log \sum_{j \in R_{r,s}}
\exp\big(z_{rj}\big) \Big],
$$

reduced over races rather than rows. Two masks carry the structure: a
validity mask marking real runners against padding, and a stage mask marking
which runners remain in the denominator at stage $s$. The row ordering
contract is paper 3's — within each race the first $S$ rows are the top
finishers in order — and it is asserted on every partition before fitting.

The loss is computed in double precision throughout, with the usual
per-race maximum subtracted before exponentiating so that scores spread over
a wide range do not overflow.

## Verification against paper 3

`scripts/verify_p5_pl_torch.R` is a standing gate, run after any change to
the objective. It asserts agreement with `R/pl_objective.R::pl_neg_loglik()`
— the function paper 3 was fitted with — on identical inputs across random
scores at mixed field sizes; the edge cases (two-runner races where $S = 1$,
races at exactly $k+1$ runners, ragged and single-race batches); depths
$k = 1$ to $4$; shift invariance; degenerate score vectors including scores
spread over 200, where a naive `exp()` overflows; and padding width.

Agreement is about **1e-9 relative**. The autograd gradient matches finite
differences to **2.9e-8** and matches paper 3's analytic `pl_grad_hess()` to
**2.9e-8**. Paper 5 therefore descends the same surface paper 3 did.

Reproducibility was checked across two fresh `Rscript` processes rather than
two calls in one session, since process-constant state can make a broken
setting look verified when re-checked in the same session.

## The two-optimiser check

Agreement on a loss value does not establish that an optimiser reaches the
same place. A linear scorer was therefore fitted in torch on paper 2b's
seventeen terms and its validation loss compared with paper 2b's own
`{mlogit}` fit on the same fitting partition — two entirely different
optimisers, gradient descent against iteratively reweighted least squares,
on the same objective and the same data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-two-optim
#| tbl-cap: "Two optimisers on the same objective and the same 17 terms, validation Plackett–Luce loss per race."
tibble::tibble(
  Fit = c("paper 2b, `{mlogit}`, closed form",
          "linear scorer, torch, Adam"),
  `Val PL loss` = c(fmt_loss(loss_2b),
                    fmt_loss(p5_diag_linear$best_val_pl_loss)),
  `Best epoch` = c("—", as.character(p5_diag_linear$best_epoch))
) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")
```

The two agree to
`r formatC(abs(loss_2b - p5_diag_linear$best_val_pl_loss), format = "e", digits = 1)`
per race. The torch fit is marginally the lower of the two, which is what a
first-order method run to convergence on a well-conditioned convex problem
should produce against a closed-form fit with a different convergence
tolerance. The implementation is optimising the objective the series
intends, not merely computing it.

## A bug a value-only check would have passed

The gate caught one real fault, and it is worth recording because of the
shape of it.

Padded slots must not contribute to the denominator. The natural way to
write that is `torch_where(mask, value, fallback)`. `torch_where()` selects
the value of one branch **but differentiates both**. Padded slots carried
$\log(0)$ in the unselected branch, so the forward loss was exactly correct
— agreeing with paper 3's implementation to 1e-9 — while the gradient was
`NaN`.

A gate that checked only the loss value would have passed this and left
every fit silently broken. The fix makes the denominator finite *before* the
mask is applied rather than relying on the mask to discard an infinity, and
the gate now asserts a finite gradient where the padding and stage masks
overlap, alongside the value agreement.
